title: How a Hole in Your Yard Becomes a Pond

lines.text: If you dig a hole in your yard and fill it with a hose, you have a pond.
But by morning, the water has soaked into the dirt, and the hole is empty again.
So you lay a rubber sheet over a bed of sand, so the stones can't poke through. This is a liner.
But a week of sun turns the water green, because algae feed on light and on whatever rots at the bottom.
So you add lilies to shade it, and plants that eat the same food. Starve the algae, and the water clears.
But still water is a nursery for mosquitoes.
So you add fish, and they eat the larvae before they can fly.
But the fish use up the oxygen in the water.
So you add a pump that lifts the water to a little waterfall, and every splash mixes air back in.
But fish poop, and their waste turns into ammonia, which poisons them.
So the pump pushes it through a box of sponges, where bacteria turn the ammonia into plant food. This is a biofilter.
But then winter comes, and the pond freezes over.
And the fish survive, because water is heaviest at four degrees. The coldest water floats up and freezes, and the deep end stays at four degrees all winter.
That is why every pond needs a deep end.
But rotting leaves make gas that gets trapped under the ice. So a small floating heater keeps one hole open. This is a de-icer.
Add stones around the edge. Congratulations, you have built a pond.
